meta.titre: Semiconductors and electronics: doping, diodes and sensors
meta.sous_theme: Semiconductors, n-type and p-type, diodes, LDR and thermistor

sections.contenu_markdown: Inside every mobile phone, torch with an LED and solar charger sold in the Mokolo market there are tiny devices made of silicon. They are neither good conductors like copper nor insulators like plastic. These materials, called semiconductors, are the basis of diodes, transistors and the sensors that switch on a street light at night. The GCE asks you to distinguish a conductor from a semiconductor, to explain n-type and p-type doping, to state what a diode does, and to use a light-dependent resistor (LDR) or a thermistor in a simple circuit.

items: Metals conduct because they contain free electrons that carry charge.
An atom of silicon has four electrons in its outer shell (valence electrons).
In a series circuit the supply voltage is shared between the components in proportion to their resistances.

sections.contenu_markdown:
**Conductors, insulators and semiconductors.** A conductor (metal) has many free electrons and a low resistance, which rises when it is heated. An insulator has almost no free charge carriers and a very high resistance. A **semiconductor** (silicon, germanium) has a resistance between the two. A pure semiconductor has few free charge carriers at room temperature, but its resistance **falls** when it is heated or lit, and when impurity atoms are added.

**Doping** is the addition of a very small amount of an impurity to a pure semiconductor to increase its conductivity.

- **n-type:** silicon is doped with a pentavalent atom (5 outer electrons), such as phosphorus, arsenic or antimony. Four electrons form bonds and the fifth becomes a free electron. The majority carriers are **electrons**.
- **p-type:** silicon is doped with a trivalent atom (3 outer electrons), such as boron, aluminium, gallium or indium. A missing electron in a bond is called a **hole**, which acts as a positive charge carrier. The majority carriers are **holes**.

Both types are **electrically neutral** overall: the doping atoms are neutral, and the carriers only make the material conduct better.

**The p-n junction diode** is made by joining a p-type and an n-type region. It conducts when the p side is connected to the positive terminal of the supply (**forward biased**) and has a very high resistance in the other direction (**reverse biased**). Its symbol is an arrow that points in the direction of the conventional current. A diode used with an a.c. supply allows current in one direction only: this is **rectification** and produces a pulsating d.c. A light-emitting diode (LED) gives out light when it is forward biased.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when asked to name the dopant, the carriers or to compare the two types
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Property | n-type | p-type |
|---|---|---|
| Dopant atoms | 5 outer electrons (phosphorus, arsenic, antimony) | 3 outer electrons (boron, aluminium, gallium) |
| Majority carriers | electrons | holes |
| Net charge | zero | zero |
| Carrier charge | negative | positive |

A good way to remember: n for negative carriers, p for positive carriers (holes).

variantes.quand_utiliser: when a diode is placed in a circuit with a cell, a lamp or an a.c. source
variantes.contenu_markdown: Check the direction of the arrow of the diode symbol: if the arrow points the same way as the conventional current (from the positive terminal round to the negative one), the diode is forward biased and the lamp lights. If the arrow points against the conventional current, the diode blocks it and the lamp stays off. With an a.c. supply, the diode allows only the half-cycles in which it is forward biased, so the lamp lights during half of every cycle (half-wave rectification).

variantes.quand_utiliser: when a light-dependent resistor or a thermistor is in series with a fixed resistor
variantes.contenu_markdown: A light-dependent resistor (LDR) has a high resistance in the dark and a low resistance in bright light. A thermistor (the type used at this level) has a resistance that falls as its temperature rises. Placed in series with a fixed resistor across a supply, the supply voltage is shared according to the resistances: the larger resistance has the larger p.d. across it. When the resistance of the sensor changes, the p.d. across the fixed resistor also changes, and this can switch on a lamp, a fan or an alarm (through a transistor used as a switch: a small current in the base controls a larger current).

sections.enonce_markdown: An LDR is connected in series with a fixed resistor of $2000\,\Omega$ across a $10\,\mathrm{V}$ supply of negligible internal resistance. In the dark the LDR has a resistance of $8000\,\Omega$, and in bright light $500\,\Omega$. Calculate, for each condition, (a) the current in the circuit, (b) the p.d. across the LDR and (c) the p.d. across the fixed resistor. Comment on how the p.d. across the fixed resistor changes.

etapes.action: Dark: find the total resistance and the current.
etapes.justification: In series, the resistances add and $I = V/R$.
Use $V = IR$ for each resistor with the same current.

etapes.action: Bright light: find the total resistance and the current.
etapes.justification: The LDR resistance has dropped, so the total resistance is smaller.

etapes.action: Bright light: find the two p.d.s.

etapes.justification: In each case the two p.d.s should add up to the supply voltage.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $8.0 + 2.0 = 10\,\mathrm{V}$ in the dark and $2.0 + 8.0 = 10\,\mathrm{V}$ in the light.

sections.conclusion_markdown: In the dark the LDR takes $8.0\,\mathrm{V}$ and the fixed resistor $2.0\,\mathrm{V}$. In bright light the p.d. across the fixed resistor rises to $8.0\,\mathrm{V}$, and this change can be used to switch a circuit.

items.erreur_markdown: An n-type semiconductor is negatively charged and a p-type semiconductor is positively charged.
items.pourquoi_faux: Both are electrically neutral. The doping atoms have as many electrons as protons. "n" and "p" refer to the sign of the majority charge carriers, not to the overall charge.
items.correction_markdown: n-type: majority carriers are electrons; p-type: majority carriers are holes; both are neutral.

items.erreur_markdown: A hole is a positive particle like a proton that moves through the crystal.
items.pourquoi_faux: A hole is the absence of an electron in a bond. It behaves like a positive charge carrier because electrons from neighbouring bonds move into it, but no proton moves.
items.correction_markdown: A hole is a vacancy for an electron, which acts as a positive charge carrier.

items.erreur_markdown: The resistance of a semiconductor increases when it is heated, like a metal.
items.pourquoi_faux: Heating frees more electrons and creates more holes in a semiconductor, so its resistance decreases. In a metal, the resistance increases because the ions vibrate more.
items.correction_markdown: Semiconductor: resistance falls when heated; metal: resistance rises.

items.erreur_markdown: Doping silicon with boron makes an n-type semiconductor.
items.pourquoi_faux: Boron has 3 outer electrons, so each boron atom leaves a hole. That makes a p-type semiconductor. Pentavalent atoms such as phosphorus make n-type.
items.correction_markdown: Boron, aluminium and gallium give p-type; phosphorus, arsenic and antimony give n-type.

items.erreur_markdown: A diode conducts equally well in both directions.
items.pourquoi_faux: A diode has a low resistance when forward biased and a very high resistance when reverse biased. That is why it can rectify a.c.
items.correction_markdown: A diode conducts in only one direction: the arrow of its symbol points in the direction of the conventional current.

items.enonce_markdown: Silicon is doped with (a) boron and (b) arsenic. State the type of semiconductor formed in each case, the majority carriers, and the number of outer electrons of the impurity atom.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Boron has **3 outer electrons**; it forms a **p-type** semiconductor with **holes** as majority carriers.

(b) Arsenic has **5 outer electrons**; it forms an **n-type** semiconductor with **free electrons** as majority carriers.

items.enonce_markdown: A lamp, a cell and a diode are connected in series. In arrangement X the arrow of the diode symbol points in the same direction as the conventional current. In arrangement Y the diode is reversed. In arrangement Z the cell is replaced with an a.c. supply and the diode is as in X. State and explain whether the lamp lights in X, Y and Z.
items.solution_markdown:
X: **the lamp lights**. The diode is forward biased and has a low resistance, so current flows.

Y: **the lamp does not light**. The diode is reverse biased and has a very high resistance, so almost no current flows.

Z: **the lamp lights, but only for half of each cycle** (it looks dimmer). The diode lets current pass only during the half-cycles in which the supply makes it forward biased; this is half-wave rectification.

items.enonce_markdown: A thermistor is connected in series with a fixed resistor of $1000\,\Omega$ across a $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$ supply. At $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the thermistor has a resistance of $3000\,\Omega$, and at $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ it has a resistance of $200\,\Omega$. (a) Calculate the current in the circuit, and the p.d. across the fixed resistor, at each temperature. (b) A fan must switch on when the p.d. across the fixed resistor exceeds $4.0\,\mathrm{V}$. Will the fan be on at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$? at $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$? Explain.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) At $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $R = 3000 + 1000 = 4000\,\Omega$, $I = \dfrac{6.0}{4000}$, so **$I = 1.5\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}$**, and $V_{fixed} = 1.5\times10^{-3} \times 1000$, so **$V_{fixed} = 1.5\,\mathrm{V}$**.

At $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $R = 200 + 1000 = 1200\,\Omega$, $I = \dfrac{6.0}{1200}$, so **$I = 5.0\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{A}$**, and $V_{fixed} = 5.0\times10^{-3} \times 1000$, so **$V_{fixed} = 5.0\,\mathrm{V}$**.

(b) At $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $1.5\,\mathrm{V} < 4.0\,\mathrm{V}$, so **the fan is off**. At $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $5.0\,\mathrm{V} > 4.0\,\mathrm{V}$, so **the fan is on**. When the temperature rises, the resistance of the thermistor falls, so a larger share of the supply voltage appears across the fixed resistor.

items_markdown: A **semiconductor** has a resistance between a conductor and an insulator; its resistance **falls** when it is heated, lit or doped.

**n-type:** doped with a 5-electron atom (phosphorus, arsenic); majority carriers are **electrons**. **p-type:** doped with a 3-electron atom (boron, aluminium); majority carriers are **holes**. Both are neutral.
A **diode** conducts in one direction only (forward biased: p side to positive); it is used for **rectification**.
An **LDR** has a low resistance in bright light; a **thermistor** has a resistance that falls as temperature rises.
In a sensor circuit, the supply p.d. is shared in proportion to the resistances, so the p.d. across the fixed resistor changes with light or temperature.
